indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Recognize the class by the -pril suffix. Enalaprilat is the intravenous form of enalapril (the injectable option in the class). Captopril has a short half-life.
indications.edu: Captopril is the short-acting member, so it is the one dosed more often than the rest of the class.

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors, continued
quinapril, ramipril, perindopril, moexipril
indications.text: Quinapril, ramipril, perindopril and moexipril complete the -pril list.
indications.edu: An agent ending in -pril is an ACE inhibitor, so the class can be named from the suffix alone.

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Most are dosed once daily; captopril is the exception.
indications.edu: If the effect wears off toward the end of the dosing interval, the fix is twice-daily dosing. The dose response is steep at low doses and flatter at higher doses, so raising the dose late in therapy gains little.
verify: Steep dose response at low doses

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Hypertension: lowers total peripheral resistance and both systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and reduces left ventricular hypertrophy caused by high pressure. Preferred in diabetics because of the kidney-protective effect.
indications.edu: Drug choice follows the comorbidity: in a patient with diabetes, this class is chosen for its kidney protection, not just for the pressure lowering.

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Left ventricular dysfunction (heart failure): reduces remodeling, afterload and preload, raises cardiac output, prevents or delays progression, and lowers myocardial infarction and hospitalization. Should be given to all patients with left ventricular dysfunction unless contraindicated.
indications.edu: Explain that the drug protects the heart over the long term even when the patient feels well.
verify: ACE inhibitors should be given to all with LV dysfunction unless contraindicated
Prevent or delay progression of CHF

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: After a myocardial infarction: reduces myocardial remodeling and overall mortality. Diabetic nephropathy: lowers glomerular pressure and prevents or delays progression of kidney disease in diabetic patients; it also slows other kidney diseases.
indications.edu: Kidney protection in diabetes is a reason to choose this class beyond the blood pressure number.
verify: overall mortality when given post MI
Prevent or delay progression of renal disease in diabetic patients

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Dry cough (5–15% of patients) is thought to come from bradykinin and substance P accumulating in the lungs. It appears from 1 week to 6 months into therapy.
indications.edu: Not related to dose or to the specific agent, so a lower dose or a different ACE inhibitor will not stop it; more frequent in women. Tell the patient to report a persistent dry cough; if bothersome the ACE inhibitor may need to be removed.
verify: Not related to dose or specific agent

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Hyperkalemia (raised potassium) is most often seen with kidney disease and with potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes.
indications.edu: Tell the patient not to take potassium supplements or use salt substitutes without asking. Anything that changes potassium is an easy question and a dangerous one.

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: First-dose hypotension with the first dose or an upward dose change. Most common in patients who are sodium depleted, have heart failure, or take several antihypertensive drugs.
indications.edu: Warn about dizziness on standing after the first dose and after each increase.

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Kidney disease: where kidney blood flow depends on angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors dramatically decrease the glomerular filtration rate. Use cautiously.
indications.edu: Start with a low dose and move upward slowly; kidney function needs to be followed.
verify: blood flow may be highly dependent on ANG II

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Angioedema (rare, 0.1–0.5%): rapid swelling of the nose, throat, mouth, larynx, lips and tongue. Usually develops in the first week and is reversible if the drug is removed; thought to be due to bradykinin accumulation.
indications.edu: Tell the patient to report swelling of the lips, tongue or throat at once.
verify: Rapid swelling in nose, throat, mouth, larynx, lips, tongue

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
indications.text: Pregnancy: fetal morbidity and mortality, with birth defects and fetal death; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) reduce the effect of ACE inhibitors.
indications.edu: Ask about pregnancy before starting and tell patients who could become pregnant to report it right away. Advise checking with the prescriber before regular use of ibuprofen-type pain relievers.

indications.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
indications.text: The -sartan suffix marks the class: candesartan, olmesartan, losartan, azilsartan, eprosartan, irbesartan, telmisartan, valsartan.
indications.edu: An agent ending in -sartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker; do not confuse it with the -pril ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors.

indications.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
indications.text: Hypertension. The angiotensin receptors are saturated at starting doses for most agents, so the dose response is nonlinear and larger doses change blood pressure little. Adding a diuretic (for example hydrochlorothiazide) increases the effect, and most come in combination form. Less effective alone in salt-sensitive hypertension, where a diuretic improves outcomes.
indications.edu: Adding a diuretic increases the response more than raising the dose, which is why most products come in combination form. In the usual stepwise plan, though, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is added before the diuretic; the diuretic is the third step.

indications.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
indications.text: Left ventricular dysfunction: used when the patient cannot tolerate an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor. Diabetic nephropathy.
indications.edu: The usual reason for the switch is the ACE inhibitor cough; in heart failure start with a low dose and titrate upward.
verify: Used when can't tolerate ACE Inhibitor

indications.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
indications.text: Same warnings as ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors: hyperkalemia with kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics, first-dose hypotension, impaired kidney function (angiotensin II is important for kidney function), and fetal morbidity and mortality: not given in the second and third trimesters.
indications.edu: Same counseling as ACE inhibitors: no potassium supplements or salt substitutes without asking; report pregnancy immediately; expect dizziness after the first dose.
verify: renal disease or K+ sparing diuretics

indications.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
indications.text: Do not cause cough because they do not affect bradykinin metabolism, and they have a lower incidence of angioedema, so a patient can be switched from an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor.
indications.edu: This is the classic stem: a patient on an ACE inhibitor develops a dry cough, so switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker. In heart failure, start with a low dose and titrate upward.
verify: start doses low and titrate upwards

indications.text: Uses listed for the class as a whole: angina, hypertension, supraventricular arrhythmias, diastolic heart failure, cerebral ischemia and migraine prophylaxis. Not every member has every use: the arrhythmia and diastolic heart failure uses belong to diltiazem and verapamil, and nimodipine is the cerebral agent.
indications.edu: Which member is chosen depends on whether the goal is to relax the vessels or to slow the heart.

indications.text: To reduce heart rate or slow atrioventricular conduction, use diltiazem or verapamil. The dihydropyridines work mainly on the vessels: their suppression of atrioventricular conduction is 0 and of contractility is 0 to minimal.
indications.edu: The exact plus counts are not the point; the pattern is: non-dihydropyridines act on the heart and vessels, dihydropyridines act on the vessels.

indications.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
indications.text: Available intravenously or by mouth, immediate-release or sustained-release. Approved for angina, hypertension, supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or flutter, and paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
indications.edu: The heart-rate-slowing indications belong to this pair only: the dihydropyridines are not approved for arrhythmias. Sustained-release forms reduce the number of daily doses.
verify: Available IV or PO (IR or SR)

indications.drug:
Amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
Norvasc, Adalat, Cardene
indications.text: Approved for angina and hypertension. Nicardipine is available intravenously.
indications.edu: Oral only, except nicardipine.

indications.drug:
Felodipine, isradipine, nisoldipine
Plendil, DynaCirc, Sular
indications.text: Approved for hypertension only.
indications.edu: Oral only.

indications.text: Approved for subarachnoid hemorrhage (bleeding around the brain), not for blood pressure.
indications.edu: Oral only.

indications.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
indications.text: Use the -dipine suffix to recognize the class.
indications.edu: Avoid short-acting formulations: they cause an abrupt fall in pressure. Long-acting products give steadier control.

indications.drug:
First-generation (non-selective) beta blockers
nadolol, penbutolol, pindolol, propranolol, sotalol, timolol
indications.text: Non-selective: block both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. Propranolol is the classic example.
indications.edu: Memory aid: in the first two generation tables, names from N to Z are non-selective and names from A to M are beta-1 selective; carvedilol and labetalol are the exceptions.

indications.drug:
Second-generation (beta-1 selective) beta blockers
acebutolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol
indications.text: Selective for beta-1 receptors: acebutolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol and metoprolol. Esmolol is intravenous only (brand Brevibloc).
indications.edu: Esmolol is the intravenous-only agent of the group.

indications.drug:
Third-generation (vasodilating) beta blockers
carvedilol, labetalol; also carteolol, betaxolol
indications.text: Carvedilol and labetalol also block alpha-1 receptors (labetalol also has beta-2 agonist activity; carvedilol has antioxidant and antiproliferative actions), giving direct vasodilation.
indications.edu: The extra vasodilating action gives these two more blood-pressure lowering than a pure beta blocker.

indications.text: Hypertension: not recommended for first-line management. Works best in young patients with resting tachycardia, raised catecholamines and raised renin; still useful in the elderly.
indications.edu: Expect fatigue and limited exercise tolerance, the common complaint. Usually chosen because the patient has another indication, with the pressure lowering as a bonus.
verify: Not recommended for first line management of HTN

indications.drug:
Timolol, betaxolol, carteolol
glaucoma beta blockers
indications.text: Glaucoma: decrease production of aqueous humor in the ciliary body.
indications.edu: Systemic effects are notable even with eye drops, so ask about wheezing, slow pulse and dizziness.

indications.text: Migraine prophylaxis (prevention, not treatment of an attack). The mechanism is uncertain.
indications.edu: Low doses may make the headache worse.

indications.text: Hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis): reduces the tachycardia, tremor and anxiety. Propranolol also decreases peripheral conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3).
indications.edu: It treats the symptoms rather than the thyroid disease itself.
verify: peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

indications.text: Angina pectoris (ischemia: oxygen demand greater than supply): beta blockade lengthens the time to the heart rate that brings on angina and prolongs exercise time until symptoms.
indications.edu: In angina, exercise tolerance improves, unlike the fatigue seen in hypertension.
verify: ↑ time to HR associated with angina

indications.text: Acute myocardial infarction: protects ischemic myocardium from norepinephrine and epinephrine, protects against recurrent infarction and lowers oxygen demand. Avoid agents with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
indications.edu: Post-infarction patients are usually kept on a beta blocker long term; they should not stop it on their own.

indications.text: Supraventricular arrhythmias: blocks the atrioventricular nodes and slows transmission (atrial fibrillation, paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia). Also used for premature ventricular contractions, which are ventricular rather than supraventricular.
indications.edu: Works like the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers on the nodes.

indications.text: Acute panic attacks (sympathetic and central effects) and benign essential tremor (blocks beta-2 receptors on skeletal muscle).
indications.edu: Blunts the physical symptoms of anxiety such as tremor and a pounding heart.

indications.drug:
Carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol
heart failure beta blockers
indications.text: Congestive heart failure: carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol. Heart failure carries a mortality of 40–50% over 3 years. Beta blockers were originally contraindicated, but in a failing ventricle they raise cardiac output and lower peripheral resistance and heart rate.
indications.edu: They initially worsen symptoms, so start with a very low dose and increase slowly. Warn the patient that feeling worse at first does not mean the drug has failed.
verify: start with very low dose and increase slowly

indications.text: Diabetes: beta blockers inhibit glycogenolysis, prolong hypoglycemia and mask its warning symptoms (type 1). In type 2 they lower insulin release and raise glucose, and can also prolong and mask hypoglycemia.
indications.edu: Warn diabetic patients that the usual warning signs of low blood sugar may be hidden; blood sugar may be harder to control.

indications.text: Sudden withdrawal syndrome: after chronic blockade the receptors are upregulated, so stopping abruptly can cause acute angina, myocardial infarction and a marked rise in blood pressure.
indications.edu: Never stop suddenly; the dose must be withdrawn slowly.

indications.text: Selective alpha-1 antagonist used for hypertension in combination with beta blockers and diuretics. Mildly lowers low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and triglycerides and raises high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol.
indications.edu: An add-on rather than a single first agent; the lipid effect is a small bonus.
verify: mild reduction in LDL and TG
Used in combination with b-blockers and diuretics

indications.text: Side effects to counsel on: orthostatic hypotension, postural dizziness, headache, drowsiness and lack of energy.
indications.edu: Tell the patient to stand up slowly. Dizziness on standing is the main complaint.

indications.text: NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) attenuate the response; beta blockers may enhance postural hypotension. Use caution in cardiac and renal failure.
indications.edu: Ask about over-the-counter pain relievers and other blood pressure medicines.
verify: Caution in cardiac and renal failure

indications.text: Treat hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. They have a longer half-life, so once-daily dosing.
indications.edu: Once-daily dosing helps adherence.

indications.text: Alpha-1A selective antagonist for benign prostatic hyperplasia, with limited effect on the vasculature (vascular receptors are alpha-1B).
indications.edu: Fewer blood pressure effects than the other alpha-1 blockers, though hypotension and dizziness can still occur.

indications.text: Advantages: efficacy independent of age, race and gender; suitable for monotherapy; works well in the elderly; no negative effects on lipids. Lowers total peripheral resistance with only a modest fall in cardiac output.
indications.edu: A workable single agent, but see the withdrawal warning below.
verify: Efficacy independent of age, race, gender

indications.text: General side effects of the class: drowsiness and sedation, dry mouth, sexual dysfunction, a narrow therapeutic range and abrupt withdrawal hypertension.
indications.edu: Never stop suddenly; expect drowsiness and dry mouth.

indications.text: Analgesic activity: blunts opiate withdrawal reactions. Decreases antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion.
indications.edu: Causes sodium retention, so it is often given with a diuretic. Dry mouth and sedation are expected.

indications.text: Less potent than clonidine and the most selective for alpha-2 over alpha-1; less sedation and only an occasional withdrawal syndrome.
indications.edu: The gentler alternative to clonidine when sedation is the problem.

indications.text: Direct arteriolar dilation lowers resistance, but the body answers with reflex sympathetic activation: tachycardia, increased cardiac output, fluid retention and increased renin. The reflex causes tachyphylaxis (the effect fades).
indications.edu: This is why hydralazine and minoxidil are not used alone: they are paired with a diuretic and a beta blocker to cancel the reflex effects. Nitroprusside is the exception, given by itself as an intravenous infusion in a hypertensive crisis.

indications.text: Chronic hypertension, given with a diuretic and a beta blocker.
indications.edu: Not a single agent: the diuretic controls fluid retention and the beta blocker controls the reflex tachycardia.

indications.text: Triple therapy for severe or refractory hypertension.
indications.edu: Reserved for hypertension that other drugs have not controlled.
verify: Minoxidil (triple therapy for severe or refractory hypertension)

indications.text: Hypertensive crisis, by intravenous infusion.
indications.edu: Emergency use only, given by continuous infusion.

indications.text: Contraindicated in coronary artery disease and ischemia; use caution in the elderly. Stools may turn black.
indications.edu: Warn the patient ahead of time that stools may turn black, so it is not mistaken for gastrointestinal bleeding. Warn ahead about any drug that changes stool or urine color.

indications.text: Hypertrichosis (hair growth) of the face, back, arms and legs. Rogaine is the topical form for hair growth; it may have cardiovascular effects.
indications.edu: Warn about unwanted hair growth before it starts.

indications.text: Given by intravenous infusion; affects both veins and arterioles. Releases nitric oxide, which raises cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and lowers intracellular calcium.
indications.edu: Only by continuous intravenous infusion.

indications.text: Toxicity comes from its cyanide groups: give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity. Thiocyanate toxicity follows long infusions or kidney failure.
indications.edu: Watch for trembling, vomiting and convulsions (cyanide), and for weakness, tinnitus, muscle spasms and toxic psychosis (thiocyanate).
verify: Give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity
long term infusions or renal failure

indications.drug:
Stepwise hypertension treatment
the algorithm on the last content slide
indications.text: Every patient gets lifestyle counseling. If blood pressure is more than 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic above goal, start an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor (or angiotensin receptor blocker) PLUS a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Otherwise: with albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 300 mg/g or higher) start an ACE inhibitor (or angiotensin receptor blocker); without it, start an ACE inhibitor (or angiotensin receptor blocker) or a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
indications.edu: Still uncontrolled: combine the ACE inhibitor (or angiotensin receptor blocker) with the dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Still uncontrolled after that: add a thiazide-like diuretic. Still uncontrolled after that is apparent resistant hypertension. This is the answer to “the patient is on this, what is added next?”
verify: Initiate an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) plus a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker

indications.drug:
Reasons to start other agents earlier
inset on the algorithm
indications.text: Thiazide-like diuretic first in osteoporosis, edema or calcium kidney stones with hypercalciuria. Beta blocker first after a myocardial infarction. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, beta blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists first in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
indications.edu: Reassess about 4 weeks after starting or changing therapy, and make only 1 or 2 titration steps before changing or adding a drug. The most common causes of poor response are medication nonadherence, the white coat effect and improper blood pressure measurement.

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: Dry cough in 5–15% of patients (bradykinin and substance P accumulate in the lungs), appearing from 1 week to 6 months; not related to dose or specific agent; more frequent in women.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about a persistent dry cough. If bothersome, the ACE inhibitor may need to be removed; changing the dose does not help.
verify: Not related to dose or specific agent
may need to remove ACE inhibitor

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: Hyperkalemia (raised potassium). Most often seen with kidney disease and in those taking potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes.
sideeffects.monitor: Check potassium. Tell the patient to avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless told to use them.

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: First-dose hypotension, at the first dose or on upward titration. Most common in patients who are sodium depleted, have heart failure, or take multiple antihypertensive medicines.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch blood pressure after the first dose and after each increase; ask about dizziness on standing.

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: Renal function impairment: where renal blood flow is highly dependent on angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors dramatically decrease the glomerular filtration rate.
sideeffects.monitor: Use cautiously: low doses, moved upward slowly; follow kidney function.

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: Angioedema (rare, 0.1–0.5%): rapid swelling of the nose, throat, mouth, larynx, lips and tongue. Usually develops in the first week; reversible if the drug is removed; thought to be due to bradykinin accumulation.
sideeffects.monitor: Teach the patient to report lip, tongue or throat swelling immediately. Stop the drug.
verify: Rapid swelling in nose, throat, mouth, larynx, lips, tongue

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: Fetal morbidity and mortality: birth defects and fetal death. Contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. This is also an FDA boxed warning (black box).
sideeffects.monitor: Confirm the patient is not pregnant before starting; counsel on contraception and to report a missed period. In practice the drug is stopped as soon as pregnancy is found.

sideeffects.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
sideeffects.text: Interaction with NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs): they decrease the effect of ACE inhibitors by blocking the bradykinin-mediated relaxation that depends on prostaglandins.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for blood pressure rising when a nonsteroidal pain reliever is started.

sideeffects.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
sideeffects.text: Hyperkalemia with kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics.
sideeffects.monitor: Check potassium, especially when a potassium-sparing diuretic is added.
verify: renal disease or K+ sparing diuretics

sideeffects.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
sideeffects.text: First-dose hypotension, and impairment of kidney function (angiotensin II is important for kidney function).
sideeffects.monitor: Watch blood pressure after the first dose; follow kidney function. In heart failure start low and titrate upward.
verify: Ang II important for renal function

sideeffects.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
sideeffects.text: Fetal morbidity and mortality: not given in the second and third trimesters. This is also an FDA boxed warning (black box).
sideeffects.monitor: Confirm the patient is not pregnant before starting; report pregnancy right away. In practice the drug is stopped as soon as pregnancy is found.

sideeffects.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
sideeffects.text: Do not cause cough (they do not affect bradykinin metabolism) and have a lower incidence of angioedema; a patient may be switched from an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor.
sideeffects.monitor: A dry cough on an ACE inhibitor is the reason to switch. In heart failure, start with low doses and titrate upward.
verify: start doses low and titrate upwards

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: Peripheral vasodilation: flushing, headache, hypotension, peripheral edema, dizziness. Negative inotropic effects: first-degree atrioventricular block, bradycardia, and exacerbation of congestive heart failure or pulmonary edema.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch heart rate, blood pressure and signs of heart failure (swelling, breathlessness).
verify: Flushing, headache, hypotension, peripheral edema, dizziness

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: Gastrointestinal effects: nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia and constipation. Elevations in liver-function tests.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about bowel habits; follow liver function tests.

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: Central nervous system effects: fatigue, nervousness, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, insomnia, confusion. Gynecomastia or sexual dysfunction, gingival hyperplasia and skin reactions.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about mood, sleep and sexual side effects; good dental hygiene for the gums.
verify: fatigue, nervousness, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, insomnia, and confusion

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: They inhibit cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), raising levels of the statins atorvastatin, lovastatin and simvastatin, carbamazepine, propranolol, tacrolimus and cyclosporine. They also inhibit P-glycoprotein, raising tacrolimus, cyclosporine, carbamazepine and digoxin.
sideeffects.monitor: Review every medicine on the list when one of these is started; watch for toxicity of the other drug.

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: Pharmacodynamic interactions: with amiodarone (slows the sinus rate or worsens atrioventricular block), digoxin and beta blockers.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor heart rate, rhythm and blood pressure whenever another drug that slows the heart is combined.
verify: Amiodarone - slow sinus rate or worsen AV block

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: Because these drugs are also substrates of cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), CYP3A4 inhibitors increase their half-life.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for more side effects when a CYP3A4 inhibitor is added.

sideeffects.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
sideeffects.text: Peripheral vasodilation: peripheral edema, dyspnea, wheezing and rebound tachycardia.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about ankle swelling and a racing heart.

sideeffects.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
sideeffects.text: Gastrointestinal, central nervous system and skin effects. Gynecomastia (reported more with nifedipine than with diltiazem, a non-dihydropyridine) and gingival hyperplasia.
sideeffects.monitor: Good dental hygiene for the gums.

sideeffects.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
sideeffects.text: Pharmacodynamic interactions with amiodarone, digoxin and beta blockers.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate when combined.

sideeffects.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
sideeffects.text: cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitors increase the half-life of dihydropyridines.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for more side effects when a CYP3A4 inhibitor is added.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: Bronchoconstriction: asthma exacerbation. About one third of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease have bronchospasm. Less likely with beta-1 selective agents.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about wheezing; prefer a beta-1 selective agent in patients with lung disease.
verify: Less likely with b1 selective agents

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: Cardiodepressive actions: negative inotropy (fatigue, heart failure); negative chronotropy (bradycardia, heart rate below 60 beats per minute); atrioventricular block: first-, second- and third-degree heart block.
sideeffects.monitor: Check pulse and blood pressure; report fainting, marked fatigue or swelling.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: Disturbed glucose metabolism: they inhibit glycogenolysis, prolonging hypoglycemia and masking its symptoms (type 1 diabetes); in type 2 they lower insulin release and raise glucose, which is hard to control.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor blood glucose; warn diabetic patients that warning signs of low blood sugar may be hidden.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: Impaired peripheral circulation: block beta-2 receptors in blood vessels, causing cold extremities (Raynaud phenomenon), skeletal muscle fatigue, and worsened intermittent claudication in peripheral artery disease.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about cold hands and feet and leg pain on walking.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: Sudden withdrawal syndrome: acute angina, myocardial infarction and a marked rise in blood pressure, because blockade upregulates the receptors. This is also an FDA boxed warning (black box).
sideeffects.monitor: Never stop abruptly; withdraw slowly. Ask about missed doses and travel.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: Central nervous system effects of highly lipid-soluble agents: depression, nightmares, vivid dreams, hallucinations, fatigue. Beta blockers in general can also elevate triglycerides, a separate effect.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about mood and sleep; a less lipid-soluble agent may be substituted. Follow triglycerides.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: With verapamil or diltiazem: synergistic falls in blood pressure, heart rate and contractility. Use lower doses of each in combination.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor pulse and blood pressure; the combination risks heart block and bradycardia.
verify: In combination use lower doses of each

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
sideeffects.text: With clonidine: further lowering of blood pressure; abrupt clonidine withdrawal produces a marked rise in blood pressure.
sideeffects.monitor: Never stop clonidine suddenly in a patient also taking a beta blocker.

sideeffects.drug:
Alpha-1 blockers
-zosin: prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin
sideeffects.text: Orthostatic hypotension, postural dizziness, headache, drowsiness and lack of energy (prazosin).
sideeffects.monitor: Counsel on rising slowly; first doses at bedtime are commonly used.

sideeffects.drug:
Alpha-1 blockers
-zosin: prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin
sideeffects.text: Mild reflex tachycardia (perhaps limited by some central sympatholytic activity and by dilation of both arteries and veins); increased renin, and sodium and water retention; impotence.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch heart rate, fluid retention and sexual function.

sideeffects.drug:
Alpha-1 blockers
-zosin: prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin
sideeffects.text: NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) attenuate the response; beta blockers may enhance postural hypotension.
sideeffects.monitor: Use caution in cardiac and renal failure.
verify: Caution in cardiac and renal failure

sideeffects.drug:
Tamsulosin
Flomax
sideeffects.text: Hypotension, dizziness and diarrhea.
sideeffects.monitor: Less vascular effect than the other alpha-1 blockers, but still check for dizziness.

sideeffects.drug:
Central sympatholytics
clonidine, guanfacine
sideeffects.text: General class effects: drowsiness and sedation, dry mouth (both central), sexual dysfunction, narrow therapeutic range and abrupt withdrawal hypertension.
sideeffects.monitor: Counsel to expect drowsiness and dry mouth; never stop suddenly.

sideeffects.drug:
Clonidine
Catapres
sideeffects.text: Increases blood glucose (inhibits insulin secretion). An initial acute pressor response (a brief rise in pressure) can occur.
sideeffects.monitor: Follow blood glucose in diabetic patients.

sideeffects.drug:
Clonidine
Catapres
sideeffects.text: Sodium retention (so it is often given with a diuretic), dry mouth and sedation (central effects); decreases antidiuretic hormone secretion.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for fluid retention and swelling; counsel about drowsiness.

sideeffects.drug:
Clonidine
Catapres
sideeffects.text: Withdrawal reactions (may be severe), orthostatic hypotension, impotence and bradycardia.
sideeffects.monitor: Never stop abruptly; taper. Check pulse and standing blood pressure.

sideeffects.drug:
Guanfacine
Tenex
sideeffects.text: Less sedation than clonidine and only an occasional withdrawal syndrome.
sideeffects.monitor: Still avoid stopping suddenly.

sideeffects.drug:
Direct vasodilators
hydralazine, minoxidil, nitroprusside
sideeffects.text: Reflex effects of arteriolar dilation: tachycardia, increased cardiac output, fluid retention and increased renin, then tachyphylaxis.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch heart rate, weight and swelling; hydralazine and minoxidil are paired with a diuretic and a beta blocker.

sideeffects.drug:
Hydralazine
Apresoline
sideeffects.text: Headache, dizziness, flushing. Reflex increase in cardiac output and fluid volume.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for swelling and a fast pulse.

sideeffects.drug:
Hydralazine
Apresoline
sideeffects.text: Hydralazine “lupus syndrome”: more likely with high dose, long-term use, women, slow acetylators and Caucasians. Hydralazine is acetylated in the liver by fast or slow acetylators.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about joint pain, fever and rash with long-term use.

sideeffects.drug:
Minoxidil
Loniten
sideeffects.text: More severe hemodynamic actions than hydralazine: cardiac output rises 2–3 times and renin release is stimulated. Myocardial ischemia from the reflexes and sympathetic activity; arrhythmias from action on the potassium channel. Minoxidil also carries an FDA boxed warning (black box) for pericardial effusion and worsening angina; it must be given with a beta blocker and a diuretic.
sideeffects.monitor: Report chest pain or palpitations; usually given with a beta blocker and a diuretic.
verify: Arrhythmias due to action on K+ channel

sideeffects.drug:
Minoxidil
Loniten; topical Rogaine
sideeffects.text: Hypertrichosis (hair growth) on the face, back, arms and legs. Topical Rogaine may have cardiovascular effects.
sideeffects.monitor: Warn the patient before starting.

sideeffects.drug:
Nitroprusside
Nitropress
sideeffects.text: Cyanide toxicity (a toxic metabolite): trembling, vomiting, convulsions. Sodium thiosulfate is given to limit cyanide toxicity. This is also an FDA boxed warning (black box).
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for the signs during infusion; give sodium thiosulfate.
verify: Give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity

sideeffects.drug:
Nitroprusside
Nitropress
sideeffects.text: Thiocyanate toxicity: weakness, anoxia, tinnitus, muscle spasms and toxic psychosis, seen with long-term infusions or kidney failure.
sideeffects.monitor: Limit duration; follow kidney function.
verify: weakness, anoxia, tinnitus, muscle spasms, toxic psychosis
long term infusions or renal failure

contra.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
contra.text: Contraindicated in the second and third trimesters: birth defects and fetal death. (In practice they are stopped as soon as pregnancy is found.)

contra.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
contra.text: Use cautiously in kidney disease: low doses, moved upward slowly, because ACE inhibitors can dramatically decrease the glomerular filtration rate where kidney blood flow depends on angiotensin II.

contra.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
contra.text: Hyperkalemia risk: kidney disease, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements and salt substitutes.
verify: Most often seen with renal disease

contra.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
contra.text: First-dose hypotension is most likely in patients who are sodium depleted, have heart failure, or take multiple antihypertensive drugs.
verify: Most common in sodium depleted, CHF or on multiple antihypertensive meds

contra.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
contra.text: NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) decrease the effect of ACE inhibitors (they block prostaglandin-dependent, bradykinin-mediated relaxation).

contra.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
contra.text: Angioedema (rare, 0.1–0.5%) usually develops in the first week and is reversible if the drug is removed. Stop the drug.

contra.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
contra.text: Not given in the second and third trimesters (fetal morbidity and mortality). An angiotensin receptor blocker is therefore not a safe substitute for an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor in pregnancy.

contra.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
contra.text: Hyperkalemia with kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics; first-dose hypotension; impaired kidney function.
verify: renal disease or K+ sparing diuretics

contra.drug:
ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers)
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
contra.text: In heart failure, start with low doses and titrate upward.
verify: In heart failure start doses low and titrate upwards

contra.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
contra.text: Contraindicated in advanced heart block and hypotension.

contra.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
contra.text: Relative contraindications: heart failure, liver disease and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Heart failure is the one to remember, because these drugs suppress contractility.

contra.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
contra.text: Pharmacodynamic interactions: amiodarone (slower sinus rate, worse atrioventricular block), digoxin and beta blockers. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) and P-glycoprotein inhibition raises levels of statins, carbamazepine, propranolol, tacrolimus, cyclosporine and digoxin.
verify: Amiodarone - slow sinus rate or worsen AV block

contra.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
contra.text: Contraindicated in severe aortic stenosis, and in unstable angina or recent myocardial infarction (immediate-release formulation).
verify: Unstable angina or recent MI (immediate release formulation)

contra.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
contra.text: Avoid short-acting formulations.

contra.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
contra.text: Pharmacodynamic interactions with amiodarone, digoxin and beta blockers; cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitors increase the half-life.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Contraindicated in bronchospasm: about one third of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease have bronchospasm, and asthma can flare. Bronchoconstriction is less likely with beta-1 selective agents.
verify: 1/3 of COPD patients have bronchospasm - contraindicated
Less likely with b1 selective agents

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Avoid agents with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity after an acute myocardial infarction.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Heart failure: beta blockers were originally contraindicated. They are now used in a failing ventricle (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) but initially worsen symptoms: start with a very low dose and increase slowly.
verify: start with very low dose and increase slowly

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Bradycardia (heart rate below 60 beats per minute) and heart block: first-, second- and third-degree atrioventricular block are listed adverse effects.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Diabetes: prolong and mask hypoglycemia (type 1); raise glucose and make control hard (type 2).

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Sudden withdrawal syndrome: acute angina, myocardial infarction and marked rise in blood pressure; withdraw slowly. Also worsens peripheral artery disease (intermittent claudication) and Raynaud phenomenon.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
-olol
contra.text: Verapamil or diltiazem together with a beta blocker (synergistic falls in pressure, rate and contractility): use lower doses of each. Abrupt clonidine withdrawal in a patient also on a beta blocker causes a marked rise in blood pressure.
verify: In combination use lower doses of each

contra.drug:
Alpha-1 blockers
-zosin: prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin
contra.text: Use caution in cardiac and renal failure. NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) attenuate the response; beta blockers may enhance postural hypotension.
verify: Caution in cardiac and renal failure

contra.drug:
Prazosin
Minipress
contra.text: Orthostatic hypotension is the main hazard, particularly at the start and with other blood pressure drugs.

contra.drug:
Central sympatholytics
clonidine, guanfacine
contra.text: Abrupt withdrawal hypertension: do not stop suddenly. Narrow therapeutic range.

contra.drug:
Clonidine
Catapres
contra.text: Withdrawal reactions (may be severe); orthostatic hypotension and bradycardia.

contra.drug:
Hydralazine
Apresoline
contra.text: Contraindicated in coronary artery disease and ischemia, because vasodilation with sympathetic activation raises the workload of the heart. Use caution in the elderly.

contra.drug:
Hydralazine
Apresoline
contra.text: Hydralazine “lupus syndrome”: high dose, long-term use, women, slow acetylators, Caucasians.

contra.drug:
Minoxidil
Loniten
contra.text: Myocardial ischemia (reflexes and sympathetics) and arrhythmias (action on the potassium channel); cardiac output rises 2–3 times.
verify: Myocardial ischemia due to reflexes and sympathetics
Arrhythmias due to action on K+ channel

contra.drug:
Nitroprusside
Nitropress
contra.text: Cyanide toxicity (trembling, vomiting, convulsions): give sodium thiosulfate. Thiocyanate toxicity with long infusions or kidney failure.
verify: Give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity
long term infusions or renal failure

killers.what: Most often with kidney disease and with potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes. Check the potassium; stop the potassium source. Warn the patient in advance to avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes. An easy question and a way to cause an arrhythmia.

Rapid swelling of the nose, throat, mouth, larynx, lips and tongue, usually in the first week; reversible if the drug is removed. Airway risk: stop the drug and evaluate. Tell the patient in advance to report swelling at once.
verify: Rapid swelling in nose, throat, mouth, larynx, lips, tongue

killers.effect: Fetal morbidity and mortality (birth defects, fetal death)
killers.what: Contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Confirm the patient is not pregnant before starting and stop as soon as pregnancy is found.

killers.effect: Acute fall in glomerular filtration rate
killers.what: Where kidney blood flow depends on angiotensin II, the drug can dramatically decrease the glomerular filtration rate. Start low, go slow, and follow kidney function.

killers.effect: Heart block and severe bradycardia; worsening heart failure
killers.what: First-degree atrioventricular block, bradycardia and exacerbation of congestive heart failure or pulmonary edema from the negative inotropic effect. Follow heart rate and watch for swelling or breathlessness; stop and evaluate.

killers.drugs: Beta blockers (less likely with beta-1 selective agents)
killers.what: Blockade of airway beta-2 receptors can trigger bronchospasm; about one third of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease have bronchospasm. Contraindicated in bronchospasm; beta-1 selective agents are less likely to cause it, so if a beta blocker is truly needed in lung disease they are the ones to choose, with caution.
verify: 1/3 of COPD patients have bronchospasm - contraindicated

killers.what: Negative chronotropy (heart rate below 60 beats per minute) and first-, second- or third-degree atrioventricular block. Check pulse; stop and evaluate for a slow or blocked rhythm. Stacking with verapamil or diltiazem multiplies the risk.
Beta blockers inhibit glycogenolysis, prolong hypoglycemia and hide its warning symptoms. Warn diabetic patients in advance that the usual warning signs may not appear.

killers.effect: Sudden withdrawal syndrome (acute angina, myocardial infarction, marked rise in blood pressure)
killers.what: Blockade upregulates the receptors, so stopping abruptly exposes them to catecholamines. Never stop suddenly; withdraw slowly. Tell the patient in advance.
Withdrawal reactions may be severe. Taper; never stop abruptly. Tell the patient in advance.
Reflex sympathetic activation with a 2–3 times rise in cardiac output causes myocardial ischemia, and its potassium channel action causes arrhythmias. Report chest pain or palpitations.
verify: Arrhythmias due to action on K+ channel

killers.what: With kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics. Check the potassium, especially when a potassium-sparing diuretic is added.
verify: renal disease or K+ sparing diuretics

killers.what: Not given in the second and third trimesters. Confirm the patient is not pregnant; stop as soon as pregnancy is found.
Angiotensin II is important for kidney function; follow kidney function, and in heart failure start low and titrate upward.
verify: Ang II important for renal function

killers.what: Cyanide toxicity (trembling, vomiting, convulsions) is limited by sodium thiosulfate. Thiocyanate toxicity (weakness, anoxia, tinnitus, muscle spasms, toxic psychosis) follows long infusions or kidney failure. Stop the infusion and treat.
verify: Give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity

commons.what: Bradykinin and substance P accumulate in the lungs; appears from 1 week to 6 months; not related to dose or specific agent; more frequent in women. If bothersome, remove the ACE inhibitor; an angiotensin receptor blocker does not cause cough.
verify: Not related to dose or specific agent

commons.what: At the first dose or on upward titration; most common in sodium-depleted patients, heart failure, or multiple antihypertensive drugs. Warn about dizziness on standing.
A first-dose effect; warn about dizziness on standing after the first dose.

commons.effect: Peripheral vasodilation: flushing, headache, peripheral edema, dizziness
commons.what: Flushing, headache, hypotension, peripheral edema and dizziness follow directly from relaxing vascular smooth muscle.
verify: Flushing, headache, hypotension, peripheral edema, dizziness

commons.what: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia and constipation; ask about bowel habits.
Vasodilation with reflex tachycardia after the fall in resistance; also dyspnea and wheezing. Gingival hyperplasia can also occur.
The common complaint when a beta blocker is used for hypertension.
Block beta-2 receptors in blood vessels: cold extremities (Raynaud phenomenon), skeletal muscle fatigue and worse claudication.
Central effects of agents that enter the brain easily; the more lipid-soluble the drug, the more these symptoms.
Postural dizziness, headache, drowsiness and lack of energy; counsel to stand slowly.

commons.effect: Reflex tachycardia, fluid retention and impotence
commons.what: Mild reflex tachycardia, raised renin with sodium and water retention, and impotence.

commons.effect: Drowsiness, dry mouth and sexual dysfunction
commons.what: Central effects; the class also has a narrow therapeutic range.
Reflex sympathetic activation, increased cardiac output, fluid retention and raised renin; the effect fades. Hydralazine and minoxidil are given with a diuretic and a beta blocker.

zebras.what: High dose, long-term use, women, slow acetylators, Caucasians.
Warn the patient ahead of time that stools may turn black, so it is not mistaken for bleeding.
Hair growth on the face, back, arms and legs; the topical form (Rogaine) is used for hair growth.
Inhibits insulin secretion; watch blood glucose in diabetic patients.
A brief rise in pressure can occur before the fall.
Hypotension, dizziness and diarrhea, with limited vascular effect.

chart.title: Antihypertensive Class Comparison
chart.sub: Every antihypertensive class side by side: how it lowers pressure, what it does to heart rate and potassium, when to reach for it, its signature adverse effect and when to avoid it.
headers: Where and how it lowers blood pressure
Heart rate, potassium and other labs

cells:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
-pril: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril
Blocks ACE: less angiotensin II, so less vasoconstriction, less aldosterone, less sodium reabsorption, less norepinephrine release. Slows bradykinin breakdown.
Raises potassium (hyperkalemia, worst with kidney disease, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, salt substitutes). Can drop the glomerular filtration rate.
Hypertension (preferred in diabetics), heart failure and left ventricular dysfunction, after a myocardial infarction, diabetic nephropathy.
Dry cough (5–15%); angioedema (0.1–0.5%).
Pregnancy (second and third trimesters). Caution in kidney disease; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs blunt the effect.
rows.notes: Flagged as a very easy exam question: anything that changes potassium (ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers raise it). Also stressed: pregnancy (ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are not given in the second and third trimesters). Two drugs you must never stop suddenly: beta blockers and clonidine. Diuretics are taught later with heart failure; here they appear only as partners (added to angiotensin receptor blockers, clonidine and the direct vasodilators). Each cell is backed by a cited source reference.

cells:
Angiotensin receptor blockers
-sartan: losartan, valsartan, candesartan
Blocks the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor: vasodilation, less aldosterone, less sodium reabsorption, less norepinephrine release. Does not inhibit bradykinin breakdown.
Raises potassium (kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics). Can impair kidney function.
Hypertension; left ventricular dysfunction when an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor is not tolerated; diabetic nephropathy.
No cough; lower incidence of angioedema than ACE inhibitors.
Pregnancy (not given in the second and third trimesters). Start low in heart failure.
verify: renal disease or K+ sparing diuretics

cells:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
-dipine: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine, isradipine, nisoldipine, nimodipine
Block L-type channels in arterial smooth muscle: vasodilation, decrease afterload, no effect on preload. Little effect on the heart itself.
Reflex (rebound) tachycardia; no effect on atrioventricular conduction (suppression of contractility 0/+).
Hypertension; angina (amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine); nimodipine for subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Peripheral edema, dyspnea, wheezing, rebound tachycardia; gingival hyperplasia.
Severe aortic stenosis; unstable angina or recent myocardial infarction (immediate-release form). Avoid short-acting formulations.

verify: Specific CCB Effects on Nodal Ca++ Channels

cells:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
Block L-type channels in vessels and in the heart: slow inward current and rate of recovery both fall, slowing atrioventricular conduction and contractility.
Slow the heart rate (bradycardia); inhibit cytochrome P450 3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising statins, digoxin, tacrolimus, cyclosporine and carbamazepine; can raise liver-function tests.
Hypertension, angina, supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or flutter.
Bradycardia, atrioventricular block, worsening heart failure; constipation.
Advanced heart block; hypotension. Relative: heart failure, liver disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease.

verify: Specific CCB Effects on Nodal Ca++ Channels

cells:
Beta blockers
-olol: metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol, carvedilol

Block cardiac beta-1 (lower cardiac output, with an acute reflex rise in peripheral resistance) and the beta-1 receptors that release renin (less angiotensin II); central effects lower sympathetic activity.
Lower heart rate; raise triglycerides; in diabetes they mask and prolong hypoglycemia and can raise glucose.

Not first-line for hypertension. Compelling indications: heart failure (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), after a myocardial infarction, angina, arrhythmias, glaucoma, migraine, hyperthyroidism, tremor.
Sudden withdrawal syndrome; bronchospasm; bradycardia and heart block; fatigue.
Bronchospasm (asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). Never stop suddenly.
verify: 1/3 of COPD patients have bronchospasm - contraindicated

cells:
Alpha-1 blockers
-zosin: prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin; tamsulosin is alpha-1A
Block vascular alpha-1 receptors: dilate precapillary arterioles and lower total peripheral resistance.
Reflex tachycardia (mild), raised renin with sodium and water retention; prazosin mildly lowers low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides and raises high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
Add-on for hypertension (with beta blockers and diuretics); benign prostatic hyperplasia (terazosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin).
Orthostatic hypotension and postural dizziness; impotence.
Caution in cardiac and renal failure; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs attenuate the response; beta blockers add to postural hypotension.

Central sympatholytics
clonidine, guanfacine
Stimulate central alpha-2 receptors (and imidazoline receptors): less sympathetic outflow, so lower resistance, heart rate and cardiac output.
Lower heart rate; clonidine raises blood glucose and causes sodium retention; no negative effect on lipids.
Can be used as monotherapy: efficacy is independent of age, race and gender and they work well in the elderly (advantages, not first-line); clonidine also blunts opiate withdrawal.
Abrupt withdrawal hypertension; drowsiness, dry mouth.
Do not stop suddenly. Narrow therapeutic range; with a beta blocker the rebound is greater.

Direct vasodilators
hydralazine, minoxidil

Dilate arterioles directly (hydralazine: mechanism not fully clear, with raised cyclic guanosine monophosphate through nitric oxide as one proposal; minoxidil: opens potassium channels, causing hyperpolarization and relaxation).
Reflex tachycardia, higher cardiac output, fluid retention, raised renin, tachyphylaxis.
Chronic hypertension with a diuretic and a beta blocker (hydralazine); minoxidil as triple therapy for severe or refractory hypertension.
Hydralazine lupus syndrome, black stools; minoxidil hypertrichosis, myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias.
Hydralazine: coronary artery disease and ischemia. Use caution in the elderly.
verify: Minoxidil (triple therapy for severe or refractory hypertension)

cells:
Nitroprusside
intravenous vasodilator
Releases nitric oxide (one nitric oxide and five cyanide groups on iron): cyclic guanosine monophosphate rises, intracellular calcium falls. Dilates veins and arterioles.
Reflex tachycardia can occur, as with other direct vasodilators; the toxic metabolites cyanide and thiocyanate build up with long infusions or kidney failure.
Hypertensive crisis, by intravenous infusion.
Cyanide toxicity (trembling, vomiting, convulsions); thiocyanate toxicity.
Limit long infusions and use in kidney failure; give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity.
verify: Give sodium thiosulfate to limit cyanide toxicity
long term infusions or renal failure

chart.notes: Two facts flagged as very easy test questions: anything that changes potassium (ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers raise it) and pregnancy (ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are not given in the second and third trimesters). Two drugs you must never stop suddenly: beta blockers and clonidine. Diuretics are taught later with heart failure; here they appear only as partners (added to angiotensin receptor blockers, clonidine and the direct vasodilators). Every cell is drawn from the Indications, Side Effects and Contraindications pages, where each fact carries its own slide reference.
